message.content:
The Britannica entry (e2250-02) defines a buttress as a mass built against the outside of a building or wall whose purpose is to prop or support it: "ferving to prop of flapper the fides of a building, wall, 6e, on the outside, where it is either very high, or has any considerable load to fultain on the other fide, as a bank of earth" [B:e2250-02]. It adds that buttresses are used at the angles of steeples and stone buildings, and along walls of buildings "that have great and heavy roofs, which would be subject to shrull the walls once, unless very thick, if no butteffes were placed againft them," and also "for a lupport and bammer against the feet of fine arches, that are turned around great halls in old palaces, abbys, cz." [B:e2250-02] (OCR errors such as "f" for long "s" are preserved as in the source.)

The matched Wikipedia article (663464@1346148586) states: "A buttress is an architectural structure built against or projecting from a wall which serves to support or reinforce the wall" [W:663464@1346148586], and that "Buttresses are fairly common on more ancient (typically Gothic) buildings, as a means of providing support to act against the lateral (sideways) forces arising out of inadequately braced roof structures" [W:663464@1346148586].

So the two sources agree on the core purpose: a buttress is built against a wall to support or reinforce it, countering sideways/lateral forces (from heavy roofs or, in Britannica's example, a bank of earth). Wikipedia is more specific about "lateral (sideways) forces" and Gothic buildings, while Britannica additionally mentions support against the feet of arches in palaces and abbeys — details not in the Wikipedia excerpt (though Wikipedia elsewhere notes counterforts for retaining walls holding back earth).
